name: Promenade Plantee
short_description: Elevated linear park on an abandoned 19th-century railway viaduct, the world's first elevated park and inspiration for NYC's High Line

beats.script_body: My Parisian friends prefer New York City's High Line to their own Coulee Verte, the first of the abandoned railroad viaducts transformed in the 1990s into a landscaped walkway above the streets of a big city. The newer High Line is wider than the Promenade Plantee, more open to the wind off the Hudson River, the plantings more diverse. Walking the Promenade from Bastille to the Jardin de Reuilly — a midway point — you have a sense of enclosure, of feeling protected along this lush corridor of flowering cherry trees, spirea, jasmine, quince. A still place, except for the play of shadows and sunlight or the slow movement of walkers, the Promenade provides plenty of benches for taking a break and enjoying the views: the small rooftop gardens of the apartments to the north that face the walkway, and the architectural facades to the south. Like a secular outdoor cloister walk that goes somewhere — as far as the Bois de Vincennes if you stay the three-mile course — the Promenade in early evening has a meditative calm.

beats.script_body: There's something thrilling about this overview of the streets of northeastern Paris, the home ground of les classes dangereuses — the dangerous classes. So much tumultuous history erupted in these quartiers below the old railroad tracks, part of the Paris-Cherbourg line. The political uproars and retreats of the arrondissements of northeastern Paris come closer to the actual character of the city — its multiple faces and voices — than the tamed tourist areas to the west. Looking down, you can imagine your own scenarios, the atrocities of poverty and injustice that once made these streets the cradle of revolution.

name: Bois de Vincennes
short_description: Largest park in Paris at 995 hectares — almost three times Central Park — with a medieval castle, zoo, and floral garden

beats.script_body: The Bois de Vincennes began, like the Bois de Boulogne to the west, as a royal hunting ground in the twelfth century. The thirteenth-century King — later Saint — Louis IX, as first judge of the realm, famously met his subjects and heard their cases under an oak tree in the Vincennes forest: 'Seated on a scarlet blanket, dressed in a simple coat of wool but with a cap of peacock feathers, [he] delivered decisions without concern for wealth or social rank.' The saintly Louis, canonized in 1297, walked back and forth between Vincennes and Paris, building a chapel in both places.

name: Chateau de Vincennes
short_description: Medieval royal fortress with the tallest medieval tower in Europe at 52 metres, once imprisoning the Marquis de Sade and Diderot

beats.script_body: The royal medieval buildings on the grounds of the château include a prison — where the Marquis de Sade dreamed of Petrarch's Laure — a castle, a fortress, ramparts, an arsenal of cannon for the defense of Paris. They were occupied by the Germans during World War II. As they withdrew from the castle in August 1944, the Germans shot twenty-six members of the Resistance and set fire to some of the ancient buildings. As you walk the long and dusty courtyard of the military grounds today, you notice there is nothing growing anywhere, not one blade of grass.

name: Parc Floral

beats.script_body: Parc Floral has been called the most beautiful flower garden in Paris. Hundreds of species flourish here: a garden of orchids from early March, a dahlia garden in fall, a garden of water lilies and lotus, a forest of camellias, a vast wavelike display of tulips from April on, fields of irises, azaleas, and rhododendrons in May. An enchanting garden, seventy-five acres of color and fragrance, with trees reaching toward the sky. Rilke's pantheistic hymn to 'the treetops, like a rising from the dead' rings true.

name: Bistro du Peintre

beats.script_body: The cafe-restaurant hasn't changed since it opened in 1902 to the artists and artisans — carpenters, cabinetmakers, ironworkers, blacksmiths — of the eleventh and twelfth arrondissements. Entering, what catches your eye first is the triptych of mirrors over the long fine bar; the incised glass behind it, the woodwork, its swirling carvings, the frescoes and little angels and nymphs in fields of flowers on the stucco ceiling — all of it original.

beats.script_body: Bistro du Peintre stands at 116 Ledru-Rollin, named for Alexandre Ledru-Rollin, a nineteenth-century radical leftist lawyer who owned property in the area. Walter Benjamin noted the effect of glass on the city around it: 'Paris is a city of mirrors. The asphalt of its roadways smooth as glass, and at the entrance to all bistros glass partitions. A profusion of windowpanes and mirrors in cafes, so as to make the inside brighter and to give all the tiny nooks and crannies, into which Parisian taverns separate, a pleasing amplitude.'

There's a museum with special exhibits — a first-rate one about Georges Méliès (1861–1938), the father of special effects, ran in spring 2008 — a café, bookshop, and film library.

However, the Library of Congress (USA) and EYE Filmmuseum (Netherlands) also claim very large collections. This is a superlative claim — per pipeline guardrails, superlatives are never auto-corrected. Flagged for user review. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cin%C3%A9math%C3%A8que_fran%C3%A7aise

flagged_claims.notes: Georges Méliès (1861-1938) is widely credited as a pioneer of special effects in cinema. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_M%C3%A9li%C3%A8s

fact_check.notes: Superlative claim ('largest in the world') not auto-correctable. Flagged as DISPUTE.

opening_hours_basis: A ticketed film museum and cinema; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Interior film museum in the Frank Gehry building with permanent collection of cinema apparatus, costumes and exhibits over several floors, roughly 60-70 min plus a ticket queue; the sculptural exterior adds a short outside stop.
judgement_basis: A film institution and cinema where quiet is expected indoors and children cannot run, with no free public seating beyond paid or lobby areas, but a large lit venue in an open riverside setting busy with people into the evening.
queue_basis: A film archive and museum with a ticket desk and light bag check but no airport-style screening, so only a minor line forms before screenings and exhibitions.

name: Buddhist Temple Lac Daumesnil

beats.script_body: Southwest of Parc Floral, across several roads, on the southern side of Lac Daumesnil near the Porte Doree metro, there's a Buddhist center, with a Tibetan temple, a pagoda, and a Vietnamese chapel. Open spring and summer only. Boating on Lac Daumesnil, you think you're in the countryside. There's a café on one of the islands.

physical_cues.cue: Tibetan temple, pagoda, and Vietnamese chapel on the southern side of Lac Daumesnil near Porte Doree metro

key_claims: Buddhist center with Tibetan temple, pagoda, and Vietnamese chapel near Lac Daumesnil
beats.source_passage: BUDDHIST TEMPLE Southwest of Parc Floral, across several roads, on the southern side of Lac Daumesnil near the Porte Doree metro, there's a Buddhist center, with a Tibetan temple, a pagoda, and a Vietnamese chapel. Open spring and summer only; infor¬mation: 01.43.41.54.48. Boating on Lac Daumesnil, you think you're in the countryside. There's a cafe on one of the islands.

opening_hours_basis: A Buddhist temple (Grande Pagode de Vincennes) entered through a door; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Buddhist temple pavilion by the lake in the Bois de Vincennes; the exterior and lakeside setting take about 15 min, and the interior with its large gilded Buddha absorbs roughly 20 min if open to visitors.
judgement_basis: This Buddhist temple building beside Lac Daumesnil in the Bois de Vincennes is a place of quiet worship where running is discouraged, offers no clear free public seating for conversation, and sits in a large unlit wooded park that empties and feels isolated after dark.
queue_basis: This Buddhist temple pavilion by Lac Daumesnil in the Bois de Vincennes is entered through open grounds with no security screening or ticket gate, so there is no line to price.

name: Sainte-Chapelle
short_description: 13th-century Gothic royal chapel with 15 stained-glass windows depicting 1,113 biblical scenes across 600 square metres

beats.script_body: In both Vincennes and Paris, Louis IX built a chapel. La Sainte-Chapelle on the Ile de la Cité remains today, a reliquary shrine of blue and flaming ruby-colored glass, its relic — the Crown of Thorns — now missing. Louis had bought it after one of his enthusiastic crusades against the heretics in the East, acquiring it from a Venetian pawnbroker.

physical_cues.cue: Blue and flaming ruby-colored glass of the Sainte-Chapelle — reliquary shrine that once held the Crown of Thorns

key_claims: La Sainte-Chapelle was built as a reliquary shrine for the Crown of Thorns
The Crown of Thorns is now missing from the Sainte-Chapelle
Louis IX bought the Crown of Thorns from a Venetian pawnbroker
beats.source_passage: La Sainte-Chapelle on the lie de la Cite remains today, a reliquary shrine of blue and flaming ruby-colored glass, its relic—the Crown of Thorns—now missing. (Louis had bought it after one of his enthusiastic crusades against the heretics in the East.) [...] see Ina Caro's 'Sainte Chapelle in Paris,' in Paris to the Past. [footnote: For the full story of Louis IX and his purchase of the Crown of Thorns—from a Venetian pawnbroker]

flagged_claims.claim: The Crown of Thorns is now missing from the Sainte-Chapelle
flagged_claims.notes: The Crown of Thorns was moved from Sainte-Chapelle and is now housed at Notre-Dame Cathedral (currently in temporary storage post-2019 fire). The book's claim it is 'missing' is somewhat imprecise — it was transferred, not lost. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Thorns

fact_check.notes: Book says Crown of Thorns is 'now missing' — more precisely, it was moved to Notre-Dame Cathedral (now in temporary storage). Not auto-corrected; flagged for editorial review.

opening_hours_basis: Gated ticketed chapel; transcribed from OSM tag "Jan-Mar 09:00-17:00; Apr-Sep 09:00-19:00; Oct-Dec 09:00-17:00" using the current Apr-Sep 09:00-19:00 season.
visit_basis: The modest facade and courtyard are seen in 15 minutes; inside is roughly 28 minutes of security and ticket queue plus 38 minutes under the two-storey glass, the upper chapel's 15 stained-glass windows being the whole point.
judgement_basis: A small ticketed Gothic chapel where silence is expected and there is no free seating for conversation, and it is locked after closing so no one can be left standing inside at night.
queue_basis: Airport-style security shared with the Palais de Justice plus a ticket check funnels visitors ahead of a small chapel, so the line runs long at midday and thins near opening and late afternoon.
